To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lipoproteins of the bacterial cell wall contribute to eryptosis, i.e. the suicidal death of red cells.

bacterial lipopeptides stimulate erythrocyte phosphatidyl serine exposure by activating the Ca2+ and the ceramide pathway, and that this process is paralleled by increased ceramide and decreased sphingomyelin content in erythrocyte membranes.

lipopeptides mimic the effects of bacterial cell wall lipoproteins and stimulate phosphatidylcholine exposure at the erythocyte cell membrane, an effect paralleled by an increase in cytosolic Ca(2+) activity and ceramide formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of bacterial lipopeptides for the induction of suicidal erythrocytic cell death.
the pathophysiology of sepsis, the life-threatening condition of the host's immune reaction to infection.
the triggering of suicidal erythrocytes death (eryptosis) by bacterial lipopeptides.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bacterial lipoproteps stimulate eryptosis in part by increasing Ca2+ activity.
Pam3CSK stimulates eryptosis in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
bacterial cell wall components trigger eryptosis by a mechanism involving Ca2+ and ceramide formation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lipopeptides trigger eryptosis, a process that may contribute to the anemia of sepsis.
lipoproteins in the bacterial cell wall may contribute to septic anemia by triggering erythrocyte suicidal cell death (eryptosis).
the triggering of eryptosis may contribute to the pathophysiology of sepsis and that the lipopeptide Pam 3 CSK 4 is a useful tool to study the pathogenesis of eryptosis.

the lipoprotein Pam3CSK triggers the suicidal death of human erythrocytes, an effect blunted by the nominal absence of extracellular Ca2+ and by inhibition of ceramide formation.
